summary.text: Abolitionism is the political movement to end slavery and free enslaved people around the world.
It gained momentum in the western world in the late 18th and 19th centuries, with Britain making the slave trade illegal in 1807 and ending slavery in its colonies in 1833.
The United States passed the 13th Amendment in December 1865, and in 1888 Brazil became the last country in the Americas to outlaw slavery.

paragraphs.heading: A movement to end slavery
paragraphs.text: Abolitionism is the political movement that set out to end slavery and free enslaved people everywhere. In the western world it picked up speed in the late 1700s and through the 1800s. France was the first country to outlaw slavery fully, in 1315, although it later made use of slavery in its colonies.

paragraphs.heading: Early steps
paragraphs.text: In that same year the French king Louis X issued a decree saying that France stood for freedom and that a slave reaching French soil should be set free. Spain, with its New Laws of 1542, became the first country to abolish and punish slavery of indigenous people. In Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi abolished chattel slavery across the country from 1590.

paragraphs.heading: Ideas and revolt in France
paragraphs.text: During the Enlightenment, many thinkers wrote pamphlets attacking slavery and the moral and economic arguments used to defend it, Montesquieu and Denis Diderot among them. Jacques Pierre Brissot set up the Society of the Friends of the Blacks in 1788 to campaign for an end to slavery. In 1791 enslaved people rose up in Saint-Domingue, the largest French colony in the Caribbean, starting what became the Haitian Revolution. Haiti remains the first and only country to have freed itself from slavery, through that revolution of 1791–1804.

paragraphs.heading: Britain and the United States
paragraphs.text: The British movement began in the late 1700s, and the Somersett case of 1772 held that slavery did not exist in English law. Britain banned the slave trade across its empire in 1807, but people already enslaved in its colonies were not freed until the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833. In the United States, Vermont abolished slavery in 1777 and Pennsylvania in 1780, and by 1804 every other northern state had followed, while the South kept it. The country banned the import of slaves by 1808, and after a bloody Civil War it passed the 13th Amendment in December 1865, ending slavery except as a punishment for crime.

paragraphs.heading: The long tail of abolition
paragraphs.text: Brazil outlawed slavery in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so. In the 20th century the League of Nations set up commissions to investigate slavery around the world and drew up treaties such as the 1926 Slavery Convention to wipe it out. The United Nations declared slavery illegal in its Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Dubai abolished it in 1962–1963, Oman in 1970, and Mauritania became the latest country to do so, by presidential decree, in 1981.

paragraphs.heading: Slavery today
paragraphs.text: Slavery and forced labour, of both children and adults, are now illegal in almost every country and banned under international law. Even so, human trafficking for labour and for sexual slavery still affects tens of millions of adults and children.
